solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Fish cut by sailor (8)

blocks.note: to cut a lesson is to skip it
jack = sailor, as in Jack Tar

annotation.surface: A fish sliced up by a sailor for supper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut' reads as something the sailor does to the fish with a knife; it means missing a class. A skipjack is a kind of tuna.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain example: the skipjack is a small striped tuna of warm seas, so fish is its category.

entries.clue: Where to see Derby County fortunate to miss kick-off? (8)

indicatorNotes.to miss kick-off: the kick-off is the first letter, and missing it drops that letter

blocks.note: Kent, the English county
LUCKY without its first letter

annotation.surface: A football fan hoping to see Derby County, who were lucky the match started without them.
annotation.walkthrough: Derby County is an English football club, so 'kick-off' feels like part of a match report. The Derby here is the Kentucky Derby, the American horse race.
annotation.definitionFit: The Kentucky Derby is run in Louisville, Kentucky, so that state is where to see it.

entries.clue: Prison on US state island bores a miser (5-7)

indicatorNotes.bores: the island drills into the middle of PER, so it ends up inside

blocks.note: pen, short for penitentiary
New York's abbreviation
inch is a Scottish word for a small island, as in Inchcolm
'a' as in 'ten pounds a head', meaning per

annotation.surface: A convict on an island somewhere in America, boring a miserly companion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bores' seems to mean tiresome; it is drilling into. The 'a' before 'miser' looks like the article of the definition, and it is really the 'a' of 'ten pounds a head'.
annotation.definitionFit: A penny-pincher counts every penny, just as a miser does.

entries.clue: Minerva St, Raleigh: Houses of the Stars (6)

indicatorNotes.Houses: the words hold the answer inside them, as a house holds its occupants

blocks.note: minervA ST RALeigh

annotation.surface: A street address in Raleigh for a mansion full of celebrities.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital H makes 'Houses of the Stars' look like the name of a building or a TV show. 'Houses' is the instruction to look inside the address.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word comes from Latin astrum, star, so it describes anything belonging to the heavens.

entries.clue: One flies equipment over base (4)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, KIT sits above E

blocks.note: kit = equipment
e is the base of natural logarithms

annotation.surface: A pilot flying supplies over an airbase.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Base' reads as an airbase in the flying picture; it is the mathematical constant e.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the paper toy on a string is made to be flown, so 'one flies' names it by its use.

entries.clue: Snoop Dogg initially detained by detective – wow! (8)

indicatorNotes.initially: at the start, so only the first letter of Dogg is used
indicatorNotes.detained by: someone detained is held in custody, so D is held inside BOY

blocks.note: busy is British slang for a police officer or detective
'Boy!' as an exclamation of surprise
first letter of Dogg, held inside BOY

annotation.surface: The rapper Snoop Dogg arrested by a detective, to general astonishment.
annotation.walkthrough: Snoop Dogg is a single name in the surface, and it has to be split: 'Snoop' is the definition, 'Dogg' only supplies its D.
annotation.definitionFit: A busybody pokes into other people's affairs, which is what a snoop does.

entries.clue: Bad-tempered wife always welcoming kiss (4)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: AY takes X in, as a host welcomes a guest

blocks.note: w = wife
ay (or aye) = always, an old word
x = kiss, as at the end of a letter

annotation.surface: A grumpy wife who nonetheless always accepts a kiss.
annotation.walkthrough: Waxy is informal British for angry; 'in a wax' means in a temper.
annotation.definitionFit: Waxy is informal British for cross or bad-tempered.

entries.clue: Discussed thin strategy to send e.g. troops back to the front (8)

annotation.definition: send e.g. troops back to the front

indicatorNotes.Discussed: what is discussed is spoken, so the answer is what the words sound like

blocks.note: reedy = thin, ploy = strategy

annotation.surface: Generals debating a weak plan to send the troops back into battle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thin strategy' reads as a flimsy plan, which suits the war-room picture; the words have to be taken separately, as REEDY and PLOY.
annotation.definitionFit: To redeploy troops is to move them again to a new position, such as back to the front.

entries.clue: Overwhelm poor Aunt Enid (8)

indicatorNotes.poor: poor suggests something in a bad state, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: Someone telling us not to overload poor old Aunt Enid.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poor' reads as sympathy for Aunt Enid; it is the instruction to rearrange her.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the literal sense is to flood, and the figurative one is to swamp someone with more than they can handle.

entries.clue: Chekhov, say, disheartened immediately (4)

indicatorNotes.disheartened: the heart of a word is its middle letter, and it is removed

blocks.note: Anton Chekhov, the Russian playwright; 'say' marks him as one Anton
the heart of ANTON, its middle letter, which is taken out

annotation.surface: The playwright Chekhov suddenly losing heart.
annotation.walkthrough: Anon is an old word for soon or at once, familiar from Shakespeare.
annotation.definitionFit: An archaic sense: in older English the word meant at once, though today it has drifted to 'soon'.

entries.clue: Maybe Georgie Porgie, Merry Henry upset with us? (7,5)

indicatorNotes.upset: upsetting the letters knocks them into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A cheerful Henry annoyed at being compared to Georgie Porgie.
annotation.walkthrough: Georgie Porgie, who kissed the girls and made them cry, is the hero of a nursery rhyme, and 'Maybe' says he is only one example. 'With' adds US to the letters before they are rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Georgie Porgie is one of the verses children learn in the nursery, hence 'Maybe'.

entries.clue: Small business shot Hershey Bar ad (12)

indicatorNotes.shot: something shot is wrecked, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A small firm that filmed an advert for a Hershey chocolate bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like filming the advert; it means ruined. A haberdashery sells sewing goods such as buttons and thread.
annotation.definitionFit: A haberdashery is a small shop selling sewing supplies.

entries.clue: Pacific location known for its controlled splashdowns? (8)

annotation.definition: Pacific location known for its controlled splashdowns?

blocks.clueFragment: Pacific location known for its controlled splashdowns?
blocks.note: the surface reading: somewhere spacecraft come down into the ocean under control
the meant reading: divers plunging from high cliffs into the sea with great precision

annotation.surface: A spot in the Pacific where space capsules come down.
annotation.walkthrough: Splashdowns in the Pacific suggest returning spacecraft. The controlled splashdowns are the cliff divers of Acapulco, who plunge into the sea from high rocks.
annotation.definitionFit: Acapulco, on Mexico's Pacific coast, is famous for its cliff divers' precise plunges into the sea.

entries.clue: Confess that hurts – wordplay gag rejected (3,2)

indicatorNotes.rejected: sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: 'Ow!' is what you say when something hurts
a pun is a joke on words

annotation.surface: Admitting that a pun fell flat and was painful to hear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That hurts' reads as a comment on a bad joke; it is the cry OW.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrasal verb means admitting to something you did, which is what confessing is.

entries.clue: Leg stump crosspiece released after payment (2,4)

blocks.note: in cricket the leg side is also called the on side
a bail is one of the small crosspieces resting on the cricket stumps

annotation.surface: A cricket scene: the leg stump and its bail.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket the stumps are the three upright sticks of the wicket, topped by two small crosspieces called bails. The whole surface is cricket until 'released after payment' turns it into a courtroom.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone on bail has been released after paying a sum as security.

entries.clue: That bloke recorded gospel song (4)

indicatorNotes.recorded: a recording is heard, so the answer sounds like the words

blocks.note: him = that bloke

annotation.surface: A man who has recorded a gospel song.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recorded' fits a singer in a studio; it tells you to go by sound.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: church songs of praise to God include gospel songs, one particular style of them.

entries.clue: London landmark cool? According to Spooner, it’s suffering (8)

indicatorNotes.According to Spooner: Rev. Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so swap the starts of the two words found

blocks.note: the Shard, the tall glass tower by London Bridge
hip = fashionable, cool
say the two words with their opening sounds exchanged

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether a London landmark is trendy, and hearing it is a torment.
annotation.walkthrough: The Shard is London's tallest skyscraper. Moving the S from SHARD across to HIP gives HARD SHIP.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a state of severe difficulty or privation, which is what suffering describes.

entries.clue: Gangly boy taking day off – November 2 (5)

indicatorNotes.taking day off: remove D, the abbreviation for day

blocks.note: LAD without its D
N is November in the NATO alphabet
the answer to 2 down, KENTUCKY, abbreviated KY

annotation.surface: A gawky lad skipping school on the second of November.
annotation.walkthrough: 'November 2' reads as a date; the 2 is a pointer to 2 down, and KY is Kentucky's postal code.
annotation.definitionFit: Lanky means tall, thin and awkward, which is gangly.

entries.clue: Rough Aussie poet eating ravioli on vacation (8)

indicatorNotes.eating: LARKIN takes RI inside, as if swallowing it
indicatorNotes.on vacation: vacated, emptied of its middle, leaving the outer letters

blocks.note: Philip Larkin, the English poet
RAVIOLI emptied of its middle leaves R…I

annotation.surface: A coarse Australian poet eating pasta while on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' pretends to be a holiday; it means vacated, with the contents gone. Larrikin is Australian slang for a rowdy.
annotation.definitionFit: In Australia a larrikin is a rowdy, uncouth young man.

entries.clue: Promising Rovers’ striker nets second (4)

indicatorNotes.nets: ROY takes S into his net, so S goes inside

blocks.note: Roy Race, star striker of the British comic strip Roy of the Rovers
s = second

annotation.surface: A promising young forward scoring the second goal for Rovers.
annotation.walkthrough: Roy of the Rovers is a long-running British football comic whose hero, Roy Race, is the Rovers' striker. 'Promising' looks like it describes the striker, and it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: when things look rose-coloured the future is hopeful, as in a bright outlook.

entries.clue: Italian corrupt politicians exercised opt out (8)

indicatorNotes.corrupt: corrupt means spoilt, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.exercised: exercised is used as excised, cut from the word
indicatorNotes.out: OPT is taken out of the letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder before the deletion
the letters O, P and T come out of POLITICIANS, leaving LIICIANS

annotation.surface: Bent Italian politicians who chose to leave some agreement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opt out' reads as a phrase from a treaty; it is the letters OPT removed from POLITICIANS before the rest are rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A Sicilian comes from Sicily, part of Italy, so is an Italian.

entries.clue: Arthur Ashe rarely conceals slice when serving (6)

indicatorNotes.conceals: the words keep the answer hidden inside them

blocks.note: arthuR ASHE Rarely

annotation.surface: The tennis player Arthur Ashe seldom disguising a sliced serve.
annotation.walkthrough: Slice and serving are both tennis shots, so the definition hides in the tennis picture. The serving is breakfast, and the slice is bacon.
annotation.definitionFit: A rasher is a thin slice of bacon served up.

entries.clue: Endlessly provoke Sinatra when name dropping Sting? (8)

indicatorNotes.Endlessly: without an end, so the final letter of the word goes
indicatorNotes.name dropping: dropping is letting fall, and N, the abbreviation for name, falls out

blocks.note: PIQUE without its last letter
Nancy Sinatra, the singer, Frank's daughter
NANCY drops one N

annotation.surface: Baiting Sinatra by mentioning the singer Sting.
annotation.walkthrough: Sinatra suggests Frank, but it is his daughter Nancy. 'Sting' looks like the musician; the definition is sting as sharpness.
annotation.definitionFit: Piquancy is a sharp, stinging quality of flavour.

entries.clue: Shake peeled seafood, upsetting the vicar? (6)

indicatorNotes.peeled: the outer letters are stripped off like a skin
indicatorNotes.upsetting: in a down clue, upsetting turns REV upside down

blocks.note: SQUID with its outer letters removed
Rev., short for the Reverend, a vicar's title

annotation.surface: A vicar trembling at being served shelled seafood.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seafood' is vague on purpose; it has to be a five-letter one whose middle gives a usable start. SQUID's inside, QUI, is the one.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to tremble with small rapid movements, the kind of shaking fear or cold brings on.

entries.clue: Sip of Cornish rum, something a bit dangerous in the main (8,4)

annotation.definition: something a bit dangerous in the main

indicatorNotes.rum: rum means odd, so the letters take a strange order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A sip of Cornish rum, which is a little risky mostly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rum' reads as the drink being sipped; it is the adjective meaning strange. 'The main' is the sea, and 'in the main' pretends to mean mostly.
annotation.definitionFit: Scorpionfish carry venomous spines and live in the sea.

entries.clue: Outcry in court as Australia lets in rapper banned in the UK (4)

indicatorNotes.lets in: OZ admits YE, which goes inside

blocks.note: Oz = Australia
Ye, formerly Kanye West, refused entry to the UK

annotation.surface: Protests in court as Australia admits a rapper whom Britain has barred.
annotation.walkthrough: Kanye West now goes by Ye and was barred from entering the UK. Oyez is the court crier's call for silence.
annotation.definitionFit: Oyez is the cry a court officer calls out to demand attention.

entries.clue: Catch terrorist at last, clear of all charges (4)

indicatorNotes.at last: take the final letter of terrorist

blocks.note: to net is to catch
last letter of terrorisT

annotation.surface: A terrorist is finally caught, then cleared of every charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charges' reads as criminal charges; it means deductions. Nett is the British spelling of net, as in net pay.
annotation.definitionFit: A nett sum is what remains after all charges have been taken off.

entries.clue: When retired, be wicked (4)

indicatorNotes.When retired: retiring means withdrawing, so the word goes back the way it came

blocks.note: to be is to exist, or live

annotation.surface: Advice to be wicked once you have stopped working.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as leaving work; it means going backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe moral badness, the answer being simply the stronger of the two.

entries.clue: That is about The Greatest Romantic? (8)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so ID EST is placed around ALI

blocks.note: id est, Latin for 'that is' (i.e.)
Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest

annotation.surface: A question: is a romantic simply about the greatest things?
annotation.walkthrough: The expected short IE for 'that is' does not fit; the full Latin ID EST does, with ALI inside after its E.
annotation.definitionFit: A romantic holds idealised views, as an idealist does.

entries.clue: Delaying hearing after arresting leaders of armed robbery (8)

indicatorNotes.after arresting: to arrest is to hold, so TRYING holds AR inside it
indicatorNotes.leaders of: leaders go at the front, so take the first letter of each word

blocks.note: a court trying a case is hearing it
first letters of Armed Robbery

annotation.surface: A trial put off after the arrest of an armed robbery gang's ringleaders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' look like gang bosses; they are first letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to tarry is to linger or dawdle, an old-fashioned word for putting things off.
